    },
    {
      "id": "obs:2",
      "text": "Plate X lists masks representing Naqumiqa otsaix, the Bear of Heaven, ALk’x’é’Lnem, and Aiq’oa’yosnem.",

      "evidence_refs": ["ev:2"]

      "text": "Nond’osqa is represented in two states, one before the birth of the flowers and one after the birth of the flowers.",

      "evidence_refs": ["ev:3", "ev:5"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:5",

    {
      "id": "obs:6",
      "text": "Another mask represents an attendant of Nond’osqa.",

      "evidence_refs": ["ev:4"]

    {
      "id": "obs:7",
      "text": "Plate X also includes masks representing A’ni’argila, identified as the moon, and the Black Bear.",

      "evidence_refs": ["ev:5"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:8",

Texts; lines 803-900","start":"803","end":"900","translation":"Tsimshian Texts","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage includes several adjacent narrative units: a hungry Giant causes sea creatures to beach themselves and eats them; the Giant later makes a garment from raven skins and is deceived by an apparent dancing blanket that proves to be leaves; an etiological statement says human beings die quickly because the Elderberry Bush gave birth before the Stone; and a Porcupine-Beaver friendship turns into dangerous reciprocal play involving a lake house, underwater travel, ice, and a tree.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The Giant is hungry, finds no food in the house, goes out in the morning, and sees ripples with salmon, halibut, bullheads, and porpoises in the water.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"A chief among the salmon says he cannot hear what the chief on shore is saying and calls Little Porpoise, who can hear it.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"After Little Porpoise relays the message, the salmon go ashore together; halibut are left dry on the beach; the Giant clubs them, takes them home, dries some, and eats others.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The Giant, being naked and ashamed, kills many ravens with a root, fastens their skins together, and puts them on.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The Giant sees what appears to be a dancing blanket, tears up his raven blanket to take it, finds only old withered leaves, then gathers and repairs the raven blanket into a smaller one.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The passage states that the Elderberry Bush gave birth before the Stone, and that this is why humans die quickly.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Porcupine and Beaver are friends; Beaver's house is in the middle of a great lake; Beaver likes the water, but Porcupine cannot swim and fears it.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"When Porcupine visits Beaver's house, he eats the food Beaver gives him, which consists of sticks.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Beaver carries Porcupine on his back in the water, dives repeatedly, and Porcupine is nearly dead with his stomach full of water before Beaver returns him ashore.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Porcupine tells his people that Beaver almost killed him, and they advise him to invite Beaver and play with him in return.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Porcupine gives Beaver tree bark and spruce needles to eat, names a tree on a grassy slope as the playing ground, sings, and speaks to the sky so that by morning the ground is covered with ice.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"At a place where water is running down and frozen, Beaver slips while Porcupine crosses with his claws; Porcupine leads content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.native-american-tsimshian-texts-boas-archive-l1471-l1558","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/native-american-northwest-coast/project-gutenberg/tsimshian-texts-boas.md","passage_locator":{"label":"Tsimshian Texts; lines 1471-1558","start":"1471","end":"1558","translation":"Tsimshian Texts","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage closes a Ts'ak' episode, in which Ts'ak' survives an attempted drowning at a whirlpool, returns with seals, and later passes through a mountain trail watched by Mouse women. It then begins a new tale about an orphaned boy whose maternal-uncle chief sees a fiery sky-object become a copper hanging in a tree; after young men fail to strike it, the boy receives secret stones from a beach visitor, knocks the copper down, and is then drawn into a new challenge involving a white bear.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A chief sends Ts'ak' to spear seals at a place located at the edge of a great whirlpool, with the chief's nephew and two slaves in the canoe.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"A great slave near Ts'ak' intends to push him into the water, but Ts'ak' throws the slave into the water instead, and the whirlpool swallows him.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Ts'ak' spears seals, fills the canoe, returns to the house, the seals are cooked and eaten by the whole tribe, and the chief stops trying to kill him.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Ts'ak' later returns by way of a mountain trail, is fed by a Mouse woman, passes through the mountain, and reaches his own house; the passage says Mouse women watch both ends of the trail.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"In the next story, a boy has lost both father and mother, and only his mother's brother, the village chief, remains.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The chief repeatedly purifies himself by drinking a decoction of devil's-clubs because he intends to give a potlatch.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The chief sees fire come down from the sky like a shooting star and hang from a branch of a tree behind his house; he identifies it as copper and promises his daughter to the young man who can knock it down.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Young men throw stones at the hanging copper all day and fail to knock it down.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"At the beach, an unnamed man gives the poor little boy concealed stones described as white, black, blue, and a final stone later described as red, and tells him not to show them to the people.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The wise men stop the young men from preventing the boy's attempt; the boy throws the stones, and the final red stone strikes the copper and makes it fall.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"A white bear is heard growling behind the chief's house; the chief says whoever kills it shall marry his daughter, and later bows and arrows are distributed, including to the poor little boy.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:9","ev:10"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Ts'ak'","description":"A named man sent to spear seals, targeted for drowning, and later returning through the mountain to his house.","role_refs":["role:1"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2","ev:3","ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"chief in the Ts'ak' episode","description":"The chief who sends Ts'ak' to the seal place and had been trying to kill him.","role_refs":["role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:3"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"great slave in the canoe","description":"A great slave standing near Ts'ak' who intends to push him into the water and is himself thrown into the whirlpool.","role_refs":["role:3"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"Drum-belly","description":"A great slave called back from the woods who returns with Ts'ak'.","role_refs":["role:4"],"evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:5","name_or_label":"Mouse woman","description":"A Mouse woman who asks Ts'ak' whether he succeeded and gives food.","role_refs":["role:5"],"evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:6","name_or_label":"other Mouse woman","description":"The other Mouse woman at the far end of the trail through the mountain; the passage says the Mouse women watch both ends of the trail.","role_refs":["role:5"],"

The boy later goes to a lake, summons a great copper-featured frog that is said to be in charge of the lake, kills it with a split-tree trap, skins it, puts on the skin, and dives into the lake.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The poor little boy asks for a bow and two arrows; the young men mock him, but wise men tell the chief to give him a bow.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Before daybreak a white bear appears behind the town; the young men run out first, and the poor little boy The prince first resists them in anger, then feeds them, marries the younger of two daughters brought for him, receives gifts, and later becomes a great chief who gives potlatches. passage says the prince's father's people were dying, while the prince's houses were full and the sea in front of his house was covered with grease.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The prince shot a gull, skinned it, put on its skin, took a piece of seal, and flew to see his father's While fetching water with the child on her back, she meets a water bull, removes sticks from its head, and is carried with her brother across the river. The old woman pursues them, mistreats the bull, and is thrown into the river and drowned. The girl later reaches her parents' camp, but the children are rejected; the chief orders them to be tied to a post and left behind, while another old woman secretly prepares help.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The little girl asks for pity and says she can work quickly and keep the household supplied with wood; the old woman agrees to let the children live for a time and sleep safely that night.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Early the next day the girl carries her after the old woman strikes the bull with her club, the bull rolls to one side, she falls off, and she is carried away and Sheltering from rain in a cave, he identifies and deceives a Snake warrior, kills him at daybreak, then receives ominous dream and visual warnings but continues on. The passage ends with a dusk view of a large camp and a lone seated figure overlooking it.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Mik-a'pi tells mourners that he will avenge Fox-eye by going to war, taking many scalps, and giving them to the widows so that the people may {
  "record_id": "batch.motif.native-american-blackfoot-lodge-tales-grinnell-archive-l4884-l4930",
  "source_text_path": "texts/public-domain/native-american-plains/project-gutenberg/blackfoot-lodge-tales-grinnell.md",
  "passage_locator": {
    "label": "SCARFACE  99 / SCARFACE  103 / I08  STORIES    OF    ANCIENT   TIMES / ORIGIN    OF    THE    I-KUN-UH  -KAH-TSI  IO9; lines 4884-4930",
    "start": "4884",
    "end": "4930",
    "translation": "Blackfoot Lodge Tales",
    "notes": "Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."
  },
  "canonical_text": {
    "quote": "",
    "summary": "Bear, the Miit'-siks chief, and the Badger chief each teach songs and dances and give ritual medicines to a man. After returning to the main camp, the man reports what he saw, and the chiefs appoint young men to bands and receive the transmitted songs, dances, and medicines.",
    "language": "English",
    "quote_policy": "summarized"
  },
  "literal_observations": [
    {
      "id": "obs:1",
      "text": "Bear says the bear is strongest and bravest, puts on a necklace of bear claws, a belt of bear fur, and a fur headband, sings and dances, and gives these and a medicine to the man.",
      "category": "action",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:1"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:2",
      "text": "In another lodge, the men are painted with red streaks and have their hair brushed to one side.",
      "category": "attribute",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:2"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:3",
      "text": "The chief of that lodge says the Miit'-siks are different from the others, are death, do not fear, and use the knife rather than bows or spears.",
      "category": "speech",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:2"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:4",
      "text": "After singing and dancing, the Miit'-siks chief gives the Wolf's friend a long knife with many scalps tied to the handle and says it is for the I-kun-uh'-kah-tsi.",
      "category": "action",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:2"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:5",
      "text": "The Badger chief teaches the man the Badger song and dance, gives him a large rattle ornamented with beaver claws and bright feathers, and two pipes are smoked in the lodge.",
      "category": "action",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:3"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:6",
      "text": "On the next day the man and his family take down their lodge to move camp, and many women give them dried meat, pemmican, and berries.",
      "category": "sequence",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:4"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:7",
      "text": "After reaching the main camp, the man feasts the chiefs, tells them what he saw, shows them the medicines, and teaches songs and dances to young men chosen for different bands, giving each band its medicine.",
      "category": "sequence",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:5"]
    }
  ],
  "figures": [
    {
      "id": "fig:1",
      "name_or_label": "Bear",
      "description": "Declares bear strength and bravery, puts on bear-claw and bear-fur regalia, sings and dances, and gives a medicine to the man.",
      "role_refs": ["role:1"],
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:1"]
    },
    {
      "id": "fig:2",
      "name_or_label": "the man / Wolf's friend",
      "description": "Receives songs, dances, and medicines from several lodges and later teaches them to the selected bands.",
      "role_refs": ["role:2"],
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:1", "ev:2", "ev:3", "ev:5"]
    },
    {
      "id": "fig:3",
      "name_or_label": "Miit'-siks chief",
      "description": "Chief of the lodge with red-painted men; says the group is death and favors the knife, then gives a knife medicine.",
      "role_refs": ["role:1", "role:3"],
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:2"]
    },
    {
      "id": "fig:4",
      "name_or_label": "Miit'-siks men",
      "description": "Men in the lodge who are painted with red streaks and wear their hair brushed to one side.",
      "role_refs": [],
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:2"]
    },
    {
      "id": "fig:5",
      "name_or_label": "Badger chief",
      "description": "Teaches the Badger song and dance and gives a decorated rattle medicine.",
      "role_refs": ["role:1"],
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:3"]
    },
    {
      "id": "fig:6",
      "name_or_label": "the man's family",
      "description": "Moves camp with the man after the lodge is taken down.",
      "role_refs": [],
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:4"]
    },
    {
      "id": "fig:7",
      "name_or_label": "women",
      "description": "Bring gifts of dried meat, pemmican, and berries to the man and his family.",
      "role_refs": ["role:6"],
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:4"]
    },
    {
      "id": "fig:8",
      "name_or_label": "chiefs",
      "description": "Attend the man's feast at the main camp and choose young men for the different bands.",
      "role_refs": ["role:4"],
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:5"]
    },
    {
      "id": "fig:9",
      "name_or_label": "selected young men / bands",
      "description": "Are chosen for different bands and are taught songs and dances and given medicines.",
      "role_refs": ["role:5"],
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:5"]
    }
  ],
  "roles": [
    {
      "id": "role:1",
      "label": "ritual teacher and medicine giver",
      "assigned_to": ["fig:1", "fig:3", "fig:5"],
      "basis": "Each figure teaches or performs a song and dance and gives a medicine object to the man.",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:1", "ev:2", "ev:3"]
    },
    {
      "id": "role:2",
      "label": "recipient and transmitter of ritual knowledge",
      "assigned_to": ["fig:2"],
      "basis": "The man receives songs, dances, and medicines from the lodges and later teaches them to the selected bands.",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:1", "ev:2", "ev:3", "ev:5"]
    },
    {
      "id": "role:3",
      "label": "chief of a death-identified knife-using group",
      "assigned_to": ["fig:3"],
      "basis": "The chief says, in effect, that the Miit'-siks are death, do not fear, and use the knife.",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:2"]
    },
    {
      "id": "role:4",
      "label": "selectors and organizers of bands",
      "assigned_to": ["fig:8"],
      "basis": "The chiefs choose certain young men for the different bands.",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:5"]
    },
    {
      "id": "role:5",

drives, notes on brush-built corrals, and the beginning of an 1881 account of bringing a distant herd toward camp.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The causeway leading to the corral was fenced on both sides by logs so that buffalo could not run down.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Women and children showed themselves around the walls and cried out to keep the buffalo from pressing against the  229 / HUNTING  231 / HUNTING  233 / HUNTING  235; lines 9643-9722","start":"9643","end":"9722","translation":"Blackfoot Lodge Tales","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical each other, sometimes fatally.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"When the commotion attracted more buffalo, Monroe signaled his men, who rode up and scared the many carcasses unskinned.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"For antelope hunting, people built long lines of rock piles or bushes in a chute shape and dug deep pits near the point where the lines joined, roofing the pits with poles, grass, and dirt.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Most people hid behind the rock piles and bushes while a few drove antelope toward the chute, and the hidden people then showed themselves and yelled so the antelope ran into the pits.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The antelope taken in the pits were killed and divided among the hunters, and this remained the common method until the coming of the whites.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Eagle tail-feathers served as a standard of value and were used for war headdresses and to ornament shields, lances, and other weapons; wings were used for fans and body feathers for arrow-making.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Eagles were seldom approached It then notes the value of eagles and briefly summarizes Blackfoot methods for taking deer, elk, wolves, foxes, and other fur animals.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"An eagle trap is made as a concealed pit roofed with juniper twigs and long grass, with a stuffed wolf, coyote, or fox skin and a piece of meat attached by a rope passing down into the pit.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"During the night, the hunter sings eagle songs, burns sweet grass, and rubs the smoke over his body to purify himself so that he will give off no scent the next day.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Before daylight, the hunter goes out without eating or drinking, lies in the pit, uncovers the bait, arranges the roof, and waits there holding the rope while crows and other birds peck at the bait.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The eagle sees the bait from the air, lands beside it, and walks toward it and onto the roof above the pit.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Watching through the crevices, the hunter reaches out, seizes the eagle by both feet, pulls it into the pit, wrings its neck, and then resets the opening to wait for more birds.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"At dark, the hunter carries the captured eagles to a special lodge outside the camp, places them on the ground in a row, and props up their heads on a stick.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"A piece of pemmican is put into the mouth of each eagle so that it will not be afraid of the people.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The passage states that feeding the eagles is meant to cause their spirits to tell other eagles that the people are feeding them.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"A human skull is kept in the eagles' lodge, and people pray to the ghost to help them get eagles.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Larger hawks as well as eagles were caught, but eagles were the most highly valued and could be exchanged in relation to the value of a horse.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Deer and elk were usually stalked singly in the brush; if not killed immediately, they were often found  257 / RELIGION  259 / RELIGION  261 / RELIGION  263; lines 10778-10866","start":"10778","end":"10866","translation":"Blackfoot Lodge Tales","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage describes Blackfeet offerings to person- and buffalo-shaped sacred stones, daily prayers to the Sun and Old Man, reliance on dreams sent by the Sun, and the summer Medicine Lodge ceremony in which a woman publicly vows to build a lodge for the Sun, prepares ritual buffalo tongues, and sponsors prayers and songs.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Near Milk River, east of the Sweet Grass Hills, there is a medicine rock shaped like a sitting man's body on top of a bluff.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"When Blackfeet pass that rock, they give it presents, sometimes putting clothing on it.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"In the big bend of the Milk River there is a great gray boulder shaped like a buffalo bull lying down, and it is reverenced by Plains Indians, including the Blackfeet, who make presents to it.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The Blackfeet make daily prayers to the Sun and to Old Man, and they ask for divine assistance before undertaking important actions.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Dreams are said to be sent by the Sun to show what is going to happen, and vivid dreams are usually obeyed, even causing a war party to turn back.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"An animal or object that appears to a boy or man seeking power in dreams is thereafter regarded as his secret helper and medicine.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The Medicine Lodge is described as the most important religious occasion of the year and as a sacrifice offered among the Blackfeet by women.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"A woman may vow to the Sun to build a lodge if a son or husband away at war returns safely or if a dangerously sick child survives; in the vow she declares that she has been sexually pure.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The vow is repeated aloud outside the woman's lodge so all may hear; if a man can impeach her claim, he must speak, and if the person for whom the vow was made dies before summer, she is not obliged to fulfill it.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"When the time for building the lodge approaches, a site is chosen and all the people move there, setting their lodges in a circle around it.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"At least a hundred buffalo tongues are collected, cut, and dried by the Medicine Lodge woman, and no one else may take part in that work.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Before the tongues are processed, the Medicine Lodge woman gives a feast to old men; an honest old man offers a long prayer for the Sun's favor, health, food, and success in war, and one hundred different songs are sung over a day and a half.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Milk River medicine rock","description":"A medicine rock shaped like a man's content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.native-american-gros-ventre-kroeber-archive-l698-l741","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/native-american-plains/project-gutenberg/gros-ventre-myths-tales-kroeber.md","passage_locator":{"label":"GROS   VENTRE  MYTHS  AND  TALES. / CONTENTS. / INTRODUCTION. / MYTHS  AND  TALES.; lines 698-741","start":"698","end":"741","translation":"Gros Ventre Myths and Tales","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Two sisters discover that Tebiaa'ta has been bringing a deer to their tent. They flee, leaving an awl and a quill-flattener by their beds with spoken instructions to misdirect him. When Tebiaa'ta returns, the decoys send him back and forth; he strikes and is wounded by the awl. He then tracks the women by their trail, and the older sister briefly delays him by making fog.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"On the fourth night the two women watch, suspect the nighttime visitor may be Naxaa'tsts', another name for Tebiaa'ta, and say he is powerful.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"In the middle of the night they see a person rolling a dead deer toward them and recognize him as Tebiaa'ta.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"After Tebiaa'ta leaves the deer and goes away, the two women begin preparing to flee.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The older sister sticks an awl in the ground by her bed and tells it to direct Tebiaa'ta to the younger sister as his best wife.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The younger sister sticks a quill-flattener by her bed and tells it to direct Tebiaa'ta to the older sister as his best wife.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"When Tebiaa'ta returns, the women are gone; only the awl and quill-flattener remain, and he complains that the deer he killed has not been touched.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Inside the tent, two bones look like women, and the voices at each side direct Tebiaa'ta back and forth between the older and younger sister.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Tebiaa'ta rolls violently to strike, but the woman disappears and the awl pierces his face.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"After pulling the awl from his face, Tebiaa'ta says the women will not escape, then looks and smells for their trail and rolls after them.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The younger sister asks the older to do something supernatural, and the older makes fog before Tebiaa'ta so that he loses their tracks for a time before finding them again.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"older sister","description":"One of the two women; she places an awl by her bed, flees, and later makes fog to delay the pursuer.","role_refs":["role:1","role:3","role:6"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:6"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"younger sister","description":"One of the two women; them in water; he receives a wife from a stranger who duplicates his own wife by striking her after four motions, but when Nix'a't imitates the act he kills his wife; and a Gros Ventre version of the Bear-Women story is summarized with local differences from an Arapaho version.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Nix'a't taunts a Bird it.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"A Night-hawk passes the rock four times while venting wind; on the fourth pass the rock breaks and Nix'a't gets up.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"After being freed, Nix'a't pulls the Night-hawk's mouth wide content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.native-american-gros-ventre-kroeber-archive-l2289-l2332","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/native-american-plains/project-gutenberg/gros-ventre-myths-tales-kroeber.md","passage_locator":{"label":"GROS   VENTRE  MYTHS  AND  TALES. / CONTENTS. / INTRODUCTION. / MYTHS  AND  TALES.; lines 2289-2332","start":"2289","end":"2332","translation":"Gros Ventre Myths and Tales","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"A young man raised by seven bulls is discovered with one of a powerful bull's wives. The powerful bull disables the seven bulls when they defend the young man, but the young man survives the bull's attack, kills him with arrows, restores his seven bull-fathers to health, and is then told to return to his human parents even though he does not want to leave the bulls who raised him.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A young Bull, described as a servant of the powerful Bull, reports that a young man, the son of the Seven Bulls, is with one of the powerful Bull's young wives.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The powerful Bull becomes angry, comes swiftly to the place, and the young man flees toward his fathers, the Seven Bulls.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The Seven Bulls say they must save their son even if they die for it, and they stand around him with their tails raised.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The Seven Bulls go out one by one against the powerful Bull, and each has his legs broken and is left unable to move.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The young man rolls up his sleeve to shoot and has a white plume on his head.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The powerful Bull tosses the young man repeatedly, but the young man is not injured; only the white plume flies up and comes down.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The young man shoots the powerful Bull from both sides and kills him.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The young man heals each of the Seven Bulls by drawing his bow, pretending four times to shoot, and making each one rise well and sound.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The Seven Bulls tell the young man that they have raised him, that he is now a man, and that he must go to his father and mother because they cannot change him into a buffalo.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The Seven Bulls escort the young man near the camp of his people; they thank him for restoring them to life, and he says he does not want to leave them because he will not know his own people.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"young man","description":"A young man identified as the son of the Seven Bulls; he survives the powerful Bull's attack, kills him, heals the Seven Bulls, and is told to return to his human parents.","role_refs":["role:1","role:7"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:3","ev:4","ev:5","ev:6"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"powerful Bull","description":"An angry powerful Bull whose young wife is human work, bodily form, and the finality of death.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The prefatory note says women take important roles married a star was torn in pieces by an Indian child.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Old Man sent Otter, then Beaver, then Muskrat, and finally Duck to dive for Man took the earth, feigned putting it on the water three times, then dropped it; afterward the above people sent rain and everything grew on the earth.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"After the flood, Old Man mixed waters of different colors, summoned all the people, gave cups of different waters to different men, and told the people to talk.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The people then spoke differently, but the Blackfoot, Piegan, and Blood, who received black water, spoke the same.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The language-changing event is said to have happened on the highest mountain in the Montana Reservation.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Old Man and Old Woman agreed that he would have the first say and she the second in deciding how people should live.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Old Man proposed easy hide-tanning, vertical placement of eyes and mouth, ten fingers on each hand, and genitals at the navel; Old Woman revised these to hard labor, crosswise placement of eyes and mouth, four fingers and one thumb, and genitals at the pubes.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Old Man proposed a floating buffalo-chip as a sign that people would die for four days and live again; Old Woman rejected agreed.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Old Man","description":"Present during the flood on the highest mountain; sends diving animals for He later slashes the birch after it holds him against a wind he has raised, misuses magical fire-leggings despite a warning, and finally turns into a pine-tree after women choosing husbands do not select him.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Some squirrels are playing a game in which one covers the others with hot ashes.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Old Man asks to join the squirrels' game and asks to cover all of them at once.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"One female squirrel, described as about to become a mother, begs to be released, and Old Man lets her meat.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Before sleeping, Old Man tells his anus to make a noise if anyone comes, and it makes noise when birds or insects squirrels.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Old Man finds the lynx sleeping on a flat stone and tries unsuccessfully to tear it in two.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Old Man bangs the lynx's nose on a rock and puts pulled pubic hair on its nose as whiskers.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Angry at his anus, Old Man takes a stick from the fire and rubs it, causing a painful burn and a bad smell.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Old Man goes up on a hill, rolls buffalo-chips down it to produce wind, and is carried along until the birch holds STAR MYTHS.; lines 2291-2393","start":"2291","end":"2393","translation":"Mythology of the Blackfoot Indians","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"A stranger gives Smart-Crow the Four-Tail Lodge and teaches him its ritual paintings and songs. Smart-Crow then gives his two sons to a rock and a beaver to raise; years later he recovers them, and they are renamed Rock and Beaver. After hunting buffalo, the brothers prepare their dead mother's lodge, boil buffalo parts, and repeatedly call to their mother until movement appears beneath the robe covering her bones.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The stranger says that hanging a buffalo-tail on the lodge will make buffalo stay near, and he transfers the lodge, ritual, and songs to Smart-Crow.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The lodge is to be marked with Dusty Stars, the Seven Stars, the Bunch Stars, a cross for the Morning Star, mountains, and four red stripes for buffalo trails.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Smart-Crow gives Ashes-Chief to a large rock to raise and gives Stuck-Behind to a beaver to raise.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"When Smart-Crow later comes for them, Ashes-Chief runs into the rock and Stuck-Behind into the beaver's house.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3","ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Ashes-Chief is drawn out with arrows, and Stuck-Behind is drawn out by a hoop-game; each recognizes Smart-Crow as father after licking his hand.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3","ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"After returning home, Ashes-Chief is renamed Rock and Stuck-Behind is renamed Beaver.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Rock and Beaver tell their father to wait in their mother's old lodge, where her bones lie, and to prepare one of her clay pots with water over the fire.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5","ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The passage explains that clay pots were shaped by hand from mud, dried in the sun, greased, heated in the fire, and then cooled for boiling.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Rock says he will boil a little meat from each part of the buffalo and make medicine for his mother's skeleton; Beaver will help with the heart, brains, and marrow.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Rock breathes on the tongue and other buffalo parts four times before putting them into the pot, while the brains and marrow are kept aside.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"After Smart-Crow, Beaver, and Rock call to the mother in turn, movement appears under the robe and her feet become visible.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"the stranger","description":"Unnamed stranger who transfers the Four-Tail Lodge to Smart-Crow and teaches him its ritual, songs, and painted markings.","role_refs":["role:1"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Smart-Crow","description":"Man who receives the lodge, gives away his sons to be raised, later reclaims them, and waits at the mother's lodge during the ritual.","role_refs":["role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2","ev:3","ev:4","ev:5","ev:6","ev:7","ev:8"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Ashes-Chief / Rock","description":"One of Smart-Crow's sons; he is given to the rock to raise, later renamed Rock, and leads much of the work over his mother's skeleton.","role_refs":["role:3","role:7"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:3","ev:5","ev:7","ev:8"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"Stuck-Behind / Beaver","description":"One of Smart-Crow's sons; he is given to the beaver to raise, later renamed Beaver, and assists in the work over his mother's skeleton.","role_refs":["role:4","role:7"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:4","ev:5","ev:7","ev:8"]},{"id":"fig:5","name_or_label":"large rock","description":"Large rock near Smart-Crow's lodge that receives Ashes-Chief to raise and later shelters him.","role_refs":["role:5"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:3"]},{"id":"fig:6","name_or_label":"beaver","description":"Beaver called Smart-Crow's friend; it receives Stuck-Behind to raise and later shelters him in its house.","role_refs":["role:6"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:7","name_or_label":"the mother","description":"The boys' dead mother, whose bones or skeleton remain in the old lodge and begin to move beneath a robe when called.","role_refs":["role:8"],"evidence_refs":["ev:5","ev:7","ev:8"]}],"roles":[{"id":"role:1","label":"ritual donor and instructor","assigned_to":["fig:1"],"basis":"He transfers the lodge, explains the ritual, and teaches the songs and painted emblems.","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"role:2","label":"father and lodge recipient","assigned_to":["fig:2"],"basis":"He receives the lodge, is identified as the boys' father, and acts in recovering them and preparing for their mother's return.","evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2","ev:3","ev:4","ev:5","ev:6","ev:8"]},{"id":"role:3","label":"son raised by the rock; later called Rock","assigned_to":["fig:3"],"basis":"Ashes-Chief is given to the rock to raise and later renamed Rock.","evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:3","ev:5"]},{"id":"role:4","label":"son raised by the beaver; later called Beaver","assigned_to":["fig:4"],"basis":"Stuck-Behind is given to the beaver to raise and STAR MYTHS.; lines 3174-3276","start":"3174","end":"3276","translation":"Mythology of the Blackfoot Indians","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage closes a star-marriage narrative: a woman and her boy are lowered from the sky to her home camp; Morning Star warns her to keep the child from touching the ground, but the warning is broken, the child disappears and is identified with a new star, and the woman establishes lodge markings and sun-dance practices before later dying after taking offerings. The passage then opens the Scar-Face tale, in which a scarred poor young man, rejected by a chief's daughter, departs to seek the Sun and is warned by a black man near a high ridge to travel only at night.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A woman and a boy are tied and lowered through a hole in the sky until the woman comes down over the camp of her own people.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"A young man with poor eyesight says he sees something coming down from the sky; his companions mock him and throw dirt in his eyes before they also see the descending figures.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Morning Star tells the woman that she will probably make another mistake and allow the child to touch the ground, and he tells her to place the sign of the Morning Star on the back of her lodge.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The woman watches the boy for thirteen days and instructs her mother to keep him on the bed while she goes for water.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"While the grandmother is not watching, the child crawls onto the ground; when the mother returns, the child is gone and only a puff-ball fungus is under the robe.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3","ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"That evening the mother sees a new star in the hole from which she had pulled the turnip and understands what became of her child.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The woman paints circles around the bottom of her lodge for the puff-ball or Fallen Star, and she had already painted the Morning Star on the back of the lodge.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The woman brings down the turnip and the digging-stick, and Crane-Woman teaches her the songs connected with them and their use in the sun-dance; this is said to be the beginning of the medicine-woman.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Many years later, while holding the sun-dance, the woman takes some offerings from the sun lodge and dies.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Scar-Face is a poor young man who lives with his sister and loves a chief's daughter; she says she will marry him when the scar on his cheek disappears and she mocks him.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Scar-Face travels far seeking someone who can remove his scar, asks repeatedly for the Sun's house, and is directed to a very high ridge.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"At the ridge Scar-Face meets a nude black-skinned man with curly hair who says the Sun's lodge is at the end of the ridge, warns him that he will be badly burned, says he lives in a cave, and advises him to travel only at night.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"the young woman / mother returned from the sky","description":"A woman lowered from the sky with her boy, received again by her people, who later paints lodge signs, brings down ritual items, and later dies after taking offerings from the sun lodge.","role_refs":["role:1"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2","ev:3","ev:4","ev:5","ev:6"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"the boy / child","description":"The child watched for thirteen days, allowed to touch the ground, then gone from under the robe and later identified by his mother with a new star.","role_refs":["role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:3","ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Morning Star","description":"The being who warns the woman about the child and instructs her to place his sign on the back of the lodge.","role_refs":["role:3"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:5"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"the woman's mother / the child's grandmother","description":"She     "quote": "",
    "summary": "Scar-Face travels to the dwelling of Sun, is received by Morning Star and Moon, is hidden under cedar until Sun takes pity on him, and is then brought with Morning Star into a sweat-house where the two boys come to look alike. After Moon mistakes Scar-Face for Morning Star, Sun gives him a new name. Scar-Face then joins Morning Star in forbidden westward journeys, kills attacking flocks of geese and cranes, and the text explicitly links the taking of the birds' heads to the origin of scalping.",

      "text": "Scar-Face travels toward the place where Sun lives.",

      "evidence_refs": ["ev:1"]
    },

      "id": "obs:2",
      "text": "The young man who meets Scar-Face says that Sun is his father and brings Scar-Face to his father's house; this young man is identified as Morning Star.",
      "category": "relationship",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:1"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:3",
      "text": "Inside Sun's lodge, Scar-Face sees an earthen square, cedar-brush, and buffalo-chips described as Sun's smudge-place.",
      "category": "setting",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:2"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:4",
      "text": "When Moon asks what he especially wants, Scar-Face says he wants the scar removed from his face.",
      "category": "speech",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:2"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:5",
      "text": "Moon covers Scar-Face with cedar as Sun approaches, and Sun orders a smudge to be made with cedar.",
      "category": "action",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:2"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:6",
      "text": "Sun looks at Scar-Face, recognizes him as unfortunate, takes pity on him, and the heat lessens.",
      "category": "action",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:3"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:7",
      "text": "Because Morning Star wants Scar-Face as a companion, Sun tells Morning Star to make a sweat-house.",
      "category": "action",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:4"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:8",
      "text": "Sun has a brass-like metal disk at the back of his head and wipes it off before bringing the two boys into the sweat-house.",
      "category": "object",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:5"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:9",
      "text": "When the sweat-house is opened to the light, Scar-Face and Morning Star look alike.",
      "category": "attribute",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:5"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:10",
      "text": "Moon mistakenly points to Scar-Face as Morning Star, and Sun gives Scar-Face the name The-one-you-took-for-Morning Star.",
      "category": "speech",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:6"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:11",
      "text": "Sun tells Scar-Face that in sky-land he may go anywhere except straight west or straight down.",
      "category": "speech",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:7"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:12",
      "text": "After Scar-Face presses Morning Star, the boys go west, seven white geese attack them, and Scar-Face kills the geese with his club.",
      "category": "action",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:8"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:13",
      "text": "Moon says she will not believe Scar-Face killed the birds until he brings back their heads, and the text states that this is supposed to be the origin of scalping and of producing proof of a kill.",
      "category": "other",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:9"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:14",
      "text": "On a later outing in the same direction, seven cranes pursue the boys, and Scar-Face uses his robe and club to kill them.",
      "category": "action",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:10"]
    }
  ],

Sun puts a cedar hoop around his head, tells him to shut his eyes, and he finds himself back near camp while people see a black object descending from the sky.","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/native-american-plains/project-gutenberg/mythology-blackfoot-wissler-duvall.md","rights_note":"Public domain source text."},{"id":"ev:3","type":"summary","locator":"3402-3413","quote_or_summary":"Scar-Face tells his chum not to touch him and to build a willow sweat-house away from camp; Dipper/Ursa Major.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The little sister meets her six brothers while going for water with her little hide in the brush, give the little sister a rabbit to take home, and plan to scatter prickly-pears around the lodge while leaving one opening for escape.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Back at the lodge, the little sister deceives the elder sister about where she has been and how she got the rabbit, cooks it, and the elder sister becomes angry when it is eaten.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The little sister leaves with her little brother, passes through the opening in the prickly-pears, meets the six brothers in the brush, and the children flee the country.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The older sister is described as a powerful medicine-woman and turns herself into a bear to pursue the fleeing children.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"One brother sprinkles a little water from his hand, and it becomes a great lake between the children and the bear.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Another brother throws a porcupine-tail or hairbrush on the ground, and it becomes a great thicket, though the bear forces its way through it.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The children climb a high tree; the bear knocks down four brothers with a thrown stick; a little bird tells them to shoot the bear in the head; and one boy kills the bear with an arrow.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The little brother shoots an arrow straight up into the air repeatedly, and each time one of the dead brothers comes back to life until all are restored.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"After a council, the children decide to live in the sky, and when the little brother tells them to shut their eyes, they all go up.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The little brother is identified as the North Star (with a question mark in the text), and the text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage closes a Big-Bear narrative by describing his rise to chieftainship, battle success, and miraculous production of water, then gives origin accounts for several ceremonial lodges and powers: the Horse-Lodge from a speaking white mare, the black-and-yellow buffalo-painted lodges from lodges seen under water, the Crow-Painted Lodge from a dream, and the Bear-Knife from a Sarcee hunter's refuge in a bear lodge during a blizzard.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"After returning home, people no longer tried to kill Big-Bear; he became kind to everybody and became a great chief.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Big-Bear killed many enemies in battle without being hurt.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"When water was lacking, Big-Bear scrunched the earth and produced water for his parents.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"A poor married man owned a white mare and a white stud colt, and the mare spoke to him while drinking and said she would give him a lodge.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The next day a lodge appeared with the white mare on its right side and the colt on its left, and the man painted the lodge with the horses, stars, earth, hills, and fallen stars as directed.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The White Mare taught the man songs and ritual inside the lodge, and the lodge was later transferred among Piegan, Blood, and Northern Blackfoot owners, with ten horses given at one transfer.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Two men making arrows by a river saw a lodge on the bottom of the water; one dived down, entered it, and found no water inside but much medicine hanging there, and later repeated the experience at another place.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The underwater-lodge experience is said to be the beginning of the black-and-yellow buffalo-lodges; the man was taught the whole ceremony, gathered the medicine, and painted the lodges.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"A man catching eagles on a hill fell asleep in his hiding hole and dreamed that a Crow gave him a lodge together with medicine, songs, and ceremony.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"A Sarcee hunter lost in a blizzard found a warm bear's den, prayed when a Bear growled, was spared by the bear family, entered a painted lodge-like interior, and the young Bear began giving him power and a knife with red paint, water, fire, and song.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:8","ev:9","ev:10"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Big-Bear","description":"A man who becomes kind to everybody, becomes a great chief, power.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"As the procession approached the river, it stopped three times and a fourth time at the river's edge, where a song about a powerful road was sung.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The husband of the Cow put the woman's mouth to the water with four movements, had her lick the water four times, gave her water with a red-and-yellow buffalo-horn spoon, fed her dried meat with four movements, and the woman was restored to life.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The husband of the Cow gave the woman buffalo-hair and told her to throw it at her husband if he remained angry, or else to make a shield for him and one for each of her two brothers.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Because the river was very deep, the buffalo made a bridge of shields over it, and the Cow told the woman to shut her eyes and later choose the first, fourth, and center shields.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"After the crossing, the husband of the Cow set the shields out before the woman, the Bull urged her to choose different ones, and she refused the alternatives four times.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"One selected shield was said to belong to the husband of the Cow and was to hang on a tripod, never be set down in the house, and always face and follow the sun.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The woman returned to the camp at night, went to her husband's lodge, and Always-Talking recognized her, welcomed her warmly, and forgave her.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Three large bull skins were used to make three shields, enemies.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"In the next account, a Piegan youth slept alone in lonely places, dreamed in a buffalo-wallow, and then instructed his ornaments.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The youth also ordered a white horse with red ears, a rabbit-like bobbed tail, and a whistle to imitate rabbit   "canonical_text": {
    "quote": "",
    "summary": "The passage contains three linked tale segments. Two men on the war-path meet a striking woman at a prairie-dog town, are taken to a lodge, and there see the Kit-Fox Society performing its ceremony, which is said to be how the men learned it. In a second segment, Chief-Speaking follows his wife's instructions, sleeps on a buffalo-drive hill, sees a procession descending from the sun, and later organizes the Catchers Society. In the third segment, a chief's daughter secretly gives birth and buries her child; four buffalo bulls uncover him, restore him to life, and grow him to adulthood. The grown man visits his people, then gains powers from both Rabbit and Hawk after protecting Rabbit and feeding Hawk with other prey.",
    "language": "English",
    "quote_policy": "summarized"
  },
  "literal_observations": [
    {
      "id": "obs:1",
      "text": "Two men are out alone on the war-path and come to a prairie-dog town.",
      "category": "setting",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:1"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:2",
      "text": "At the prairie-dog town the men see a woman with a red-painted face, a robe, a plume on her head, and a prairie-turnip in her mouth.",
      "category": "attribute",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:1"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:3",
      "text": "The woman tells the men to shut their eyes, and when they open them they are beside a lodge where the Kit-Fox Society is gathered.",
      "category": "sequence",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:1"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:4",
      "text": "A Kit-Fox man directs the others through the whole ritual, and the text states that this is how the men learned it.",
      "category": "action",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:1"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:5",
      "text": "Chief-Speaking's wife says she found the buffalo-rock and tells him to sleep on the buffalo-drive hill so that he may receive a dream.",
      "category": "speech",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:2"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:6",
      "text": "After seven days on the hill, Chief-Speaking hears singing and sees a procession coming down from the sun; two leaders carry pipes and the others carry clubs with hoof rattles.",
      "category": "action",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:2"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:7",
      "text": "After this vision, Chief-Speaking organizes the Catchers Society, and his wife places some buffalo-rock songs into the ritual.",
      "category": "sequence",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:2"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:8",
      "text": "A chief's daughter, said not to have been with any man, becomes pregnant, gives birth away from camp, and buries her baby boy in the earth.",
      "category": "action",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:3"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:9",
      "text": "Four buffalo bulls uncover the buried child, restore him to life, and successively bring him to full-grown manhood.",
      "category": "sequence",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:4"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:10",
      "text": "The restored young man visits his people, tells them his story, and receives clothes, a horse, and a bow with arrows.",
      "category": "relationship",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:5"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:11",
      "text": "Rabbit asks the man for protection and offers power; Hawk also offers power if allowed to take Rabbit; the man saves Rabbit, gives Hawk a squirrel instead, and receives powers from both animals.",
      "category": "sequence",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:6", "ev:7"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:12",
      "text": "An editorial note says a similar tale among the Arapaho and Gros Ventre has seven bulls, and it also mentions another tale in this collection and a Crow rendering with different numbers of bulls.",
      "category": "other",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:8"]
    }
  ],

The passage then shifts to the opening of \"The Lost Children,\" where a boy is denied shells by other children and his father orders the camp moved, leaving them behind.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The husband tracks the runaway wife and her companion to their camp and watches from a him.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The transferred method includes killing a coyote for bait, orienting its head to the sun and feet to the north, singing, and It then tells of a beautiful woman taken by a snake-man to an underground dwelling, returned with taboos and obligations, and later dying and disappearing back to the snakes after breaking one prohibition. The passage ends with the opening of a new tale about a sought-after young woman who notices an unusual pile of human ways and appears to be a man again.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Wolves and coyotes become as people and live in a large camp, and the chief of the wolves {
  "record_id": "batch.motif.native-american-mythology-blackfoot-wissler-duvall-archive-l8550-l8668",
  "source_text_path": "texts/public-domain/native-american-plains/project-gutenberg/mythology-blackfoot-wissler-duvall.md",
  "passage_locator": {
    "label": "ILLUSTRATIONS. / INTRODUCTION. / I. ETHNOLOGY. / HISTORY AND GEOGRAPHY.; lines 8550-8668",
    "start": "8550",
    "end": "8668",
    "translation": "Mythology of the Blackfoot Indians",
    "notes": "Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."
  },
  "canonical_text": {
    "quote": "",
    "summary": "Ethnographic and historical overview of the Shoshone, describing their geographic range, early contact with explorers and traders, alliances and hostilities with neighboring tribes, later relations with whites and reservations, and affiliations with Bannock and Comanche.",
    "language": "English",
    "quote_policy": "summarized"
  },
  "literal_observations": [
    {
      "id": "obs:1",
      "text": "The passage identifies the Shoshone, or Snakes, as the northernmost division of the Shoshonean family.",
      "category": "attribute",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:1"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:2",
      "text": "The Shoshone are said to have occupied territory across western Wyoming and Montana, central and southern Idaho, northern Utah and Nevada, and most of Oregon, with specific valleys, rivers, and mountains named.",
      "category": "setting",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:1"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:3",
      "text": "Lewis and Clark encountered the Shoshone in 1805 and inferred from native statements and riding gear that the Shoshone had already had contact with Spanish traders.",
      "category": "sequence",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:2"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:4",
      "text": "Early accounts described the Datcl'ba (Tushepaws) as the only constant allies of the Snakes, while the Bannock were said to be non-hostile but not protective in the early period.",
      "category": "relationship",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:3"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:5",
      "text": "The passage lists many tribes as hostile to the Shoshone at different times and states that relations with some groups, such as the Crow and Ute, alternated between hostility and peace.",
      "category": "relationship",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:4", "ev:5"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:6",
      "text": "Relations with whites are described as almost uniformly amicable except for local disturbances; the Lemhi remained neutral in 1877, and the Shoshone are said to be confined to three reservations.",
      "category": "sequence",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:6"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:7",

canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage describes Shoshone and Lemhi games: a hand-game using hidden marked and plain sticks, singing, guessing, and tally-sticks; dice games using marked willow sticks thrown on a flat stone and wagered with counters; and athletic contests including races, kicking, wrestling, and shot-putting.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"In the hand-game, one or two players are on each side, kneeling opposite each other, and the players are ordinarily all of the same sex.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The hand-game uses two small bones or sticks, one wrapped with sinew or string and one plain; the player hides one in each hand under a blanket, sings, and moves the arms while the opponent guesses which hand holds the plain piece.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Correct and incorrect guesses determine whether play changes hands and whether tally-sticks are surrendered; when two pairs play, the number of counters lost or gained depends on how many plain pieces are correctly identified.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"A spectator may sit next to a performer and strike a piece of tin with a stick as accompaniment to the chant, and seated spectators may also join in swinging their arms and singing.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Women in the hand-game swing both arms in the same direction, while men move their hands from in front of the shoulders toward and past each other and back again.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Beaver testicles and excrements were formerly said to be used as charms to ensure success at the hand-game.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"One Lemhi dice game uses four long, thin willow sticks with grooves and burned marks, thrown on a flat stone; another uses similar sticks with a red-painted groove and different marks.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"In dice betting, players wager counters against a target number of points, compare throws, and settle the stake according to whether the second throw equals, exceeds, or falls short of the first; some throws have special names such as do'ca and tQ'tai.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5","ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Athletic games included foot-races, horse-races around a stick marking the half-goal, a kicking game without betting or a winning side, wrestling, and shot-putting, with bets made on shot-putting.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"hand-game performer","description":"A player who hides the two sticks, sings, and moves the arms during play.","role_refs":["role:1"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:3"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"hand-game opponent","description":"The opposing player who watches the singer's hands and indicates the hand thought to conceal the plain piece.","role_refs":["role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"spectator-accompanist","description":"A spectator seated beside a performer who may strike tin with a stick and may join in arm-swinging and singing.","role_refs":["role:3"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:3"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"dice player","description":"A gambler who throws marked willow-stick dice on a flat stone and wagers counters or tally-sticks on the result.","role_refs":["role:4"],"evidence_refs":["ev:4","ev:5","ev:6"]},{"id":"fig:5","name_or_label":"athletic contestants","description":"Participants in races, kicking matches, wrestling, and shot-putting; the kicking game players are described as mostly boys and young from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage discusses several dances and associated customs: a possible but disputed resemblance between the nu'akin and ghost-dance songs; fish-increase and first-salmon observances involving paint, feasting, sharing, and taboo; the Father's dance and another older circle dance; the wo'ho-nokakin, its rasp instrument, partner celebrated to insure the coming of fish.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"At the first salmon catch, all members of the band painted with bi'cap, held a feast, and divided the first catch among all tribesmen.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"A reported fishing-season ceremony required prayers or signs over one fish before any were eaten; breaking the rule was believed to bring ill luck or death.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The a'po-no'kakin was danced like the nu'akin, used misfortune.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:9","ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"During the wo'ho-nokakin, four to six couples danced at a time, spectators sang wordless songs, partners {"record_id":"batch.motif.native-american-mythology-blackfoot-wissler-duvall-archive-l11443-l11528","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/native-american-plains/project-gutenberg/mythology-blackfoot-wissler-duvall.md","passage_locator":{"label":"SOCIAL ORGANIZATION. / VARIOUS CUSTOMS. / DANCES. / RELIGION.; lines 11443-11528","start":"11443","end":"11528","translation":"Mythology of the Blackfoot Indians","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage describes household herbal remedies, then explains illness as spirit intrusion in many cases and outlines the work of medicine-men, including dream-prompted consultation, specialist practitioners, suction extraction of an evil spirit, a Ute parallel rite using an eagle claw, and the payment and inherited continuation of healing practice.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Ordinary sickness is treated with plant and household remedies, including sagebrush, ba'gwina, spruce needles or bark, sweet-grass, buffalo horn preparations, willow splints, and herbal poultices.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"When ordinary remedies fail, the sick person decides to call a medicine-man, and this decision usually follows a dream.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"In most cases disease is explained as a dzo'ap, or ghost, entering the patient's body.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The passage reports three practitioners at the time of observation: two men and one woman.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The female practitioner was said by some white informants to practice hypnotism, but Shoshone testimony about this was contradictory.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"One male doctor was said to cure rattlesnake bites, and Tu'mo-dzo, a hunchback, specialized in sexual troubles and barrenness and was said to carry his medicine in his hump.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Tu'mo-dzo was said to treat gonorrhea by sucking the diseased part and then expectorating; women were treated similarly.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Medicine-men commonly used incantations and sweat-lodges.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"To extract the dzo'ap, the doctor formed a tube with his hands, sucked at the patient's mouth until the patient retched and belched forth the spirit, then showed it as blood or a small object and rubbed it between his palms to kill it.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"A Ute doctor was described as driving away the evil spirit by laying the patient on the ground and scarifying from head to heel with an eagle claw while men sang an incantation.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Doctors might be paid a dollar or a horse, could charm arrows for hunting and give shields supernatural virtues, and were not said to cause sickness or death among fellow tribesmen.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Sons or nephews of physicians sometimes followed the same profession.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Sick person or patient","description":"The afflicted person whose illness is first treated with remedies and later by a medicine-man.","role_refs":["role:1"],"evidence_refs":["ev:3","ev:8"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Medicine-man or doctor","description":"A practitioner called when ordinary remedies fail; performs healing rites and may have additional powers related to arrows and shields.","role_refs":["role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:3","ev:8","ev:10"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"dzo'ap or evil spirit","description":"A ghost or intrusive being said to enter the patient's body and cause illness.","role_refs":["role:3"],"evidence_refs":["ev:4","ev:8"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"Female practitioner","description":"One of the three practitioners; reported by some informants to induce sleep, though the claim was disputed.","role_refs":["role:2","role:4"],"evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"fig:5","name_or_label":"Rattlesnake-bite specialist","description":"One of the doctors, said to cure rattlesnake bites.","role_refs":["role:2","role:6"],"evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"fig:6","name_or_label":"Tu'mo-dzo","description":"A hunchback doctor specializing in sexual troubles and barrenness; described as carrying medicine in his hump and treating venereal disease by suction.","role_refs":["role:2","role:5"],"evidence_refs":["ev:6","ev:7"]},{"id":"fig:7","name_or_label":"Ute doctor","description":"A healer who drives away the evil spirit by scarifying the patient practitioners treating illness.","evidence_refs":["ev:5","ev:6","ev:8","ev:9"]},{"id":"role:3","label":"intrusive disease-spirit","assigned_to":["fig:3"],"basis":"The dzo'ap is said to enter the body perform movements that induced sleep.","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"role:5","label":"sexual and fertility specialist","assigned_to":["fig:6"],"basis":"Tu'mo-dzo was said to treat sexual troubles,
