{"record_id":"batch.motif.native-american-mythology-blackfoot-wissler-duvall-archive-l11530-l11592","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/native-american-plains/project-gutenberg/mythology-blackfoot-wissler-duvall.md","passage_locator":{"label":"SOCIAL ORGANIZATION. / VARIOUS CUSTOMS. / DANCES. / RELIGION.; lines 11530-11592","start":"11530","end":"11592","translation":"Mythology of the Blackfoot Indians","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage reports cases where healing fails, explanations for illness and death involving loss of mind or mu'gua, Coyote as a disguised taker of life, several protective amulets, a sacred stone, an evil charm made with rattlesnake heads and heated animal parts, and love-charms that attract or kill women.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Ko'bitsak explained his little girl's death by saying that a whirlwind caught her and whirled out her brains.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Tu'-dzomo-n-d5'mi refused Dr. Murphy's treatment, said he would die in three days, and died on the third day.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The passage gives two general reasons for failure to heal: a dzo'ap may enter a patient's body and carry away his mind, or Coyote may descend from above and carry off a man's mu'gua, causing insanity or death.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"In this role, Coyote disguises himself as an Indian and is recognizable only by his eyes.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Protective charms include powdered spruce needles in a buckskin bag hung around a baby's neck, white weaselskins or a white weasel foot, buffalo horns and manes, obsidian pieces kept in a bag for eye-disease prevention, and a spear-grass charm tied to a necklace.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"A sacred stone is mentioned as a tribal medicine by which good or evil could be wrought.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"An evil charm is prepared by placing rattlesnake heads on hot coals in a hole, covering them with fresh liver and gall of wild animals, preserving the treated liver in a buckskin bag, and using it with fixed gaze and evil incantations to cause a victim's death.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Love-charms include a weasel foot worn on a hat, wood or bark shavings rubbed on the neck or carried in a bag or cloth, and spruce needles chewed and rubbed on the head.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"A small inedible root glued to a little stone is thrown at a desired woman, and several nights later she is said to come to the man, look into his eyes, and laugh.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"A Ross Fork Shoshone paid Ko'bitsak for the roots, and Jack later saw him married and attributed the marriage to the medicine.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Lame-Jack says another root also called wai'i-pe-na'dcu will kill a woman in about ten days if dropped in her path.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Ko'bitsak","description":"A medicine-man who explained his daughter's death, used woman-medicine, and supplied love-charm roots.","role_refs":["role:1","role:7","role:8"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:8","ev:9","ev:10"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Ko'bitsak's little girl","description":"A child whose death was explained as the result of a whirlwind.","role_refs":["role:3"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Dr. Murphy","description":"A doctor whose services were declined by Tu'-dzomo-n-d5'mi.","role_refs":["role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"Tu'-dzomo-n-d5'mi","description":"The younger of two medicine-men; he became sick, predicted his death in three days, refused white medicine, and died on the third day.","role_refs":["role:1","role:3"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"fig:5","name_or_label":"dzo'ap","description":"A being said to enter a patient's body, snatch away his mind, and fly away with it.","role_refs":["role:4"],"evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"fig:6","name_or_label":"Coyote","description":"A being who descends from above, carries off a man's mu'gua, may cause insanity or death, and disguises himself as an Indian.","role_refs":["role:4","role:5"],"evidence_refs":["ev:3","ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:7","name_or_label":"Jack Grouse","description":"A man who says that an abusive nearby farmer was dispatched by Coyote.","role_refs":["role:6"],"evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"fig:8","name_or_label":"Jack","description":"A man who repeatedly used the root-and-stone love charm and attributed a later marriage to the medicine.","role_refs":["role:6","role:8"],"evidence_refs":["ev:9","ev:10"]},{"id":"fig:9","name_or_label":"abusive farmer","description":"A nearby farmer said to have abused Indians and to have been dispatched by Coyote.","role_refs":["role:9"],"evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"fig:10","name_or_label":"very old woman","description":"An old woman who kept two small irregular obsidian pieces in a bag to prevent eye-disease and sometimes scratched her arm with them.","role_refs":["role:7"],"evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"fig:11","name_or_label":"one man with spear-grass charm","description":"A man who carried spear-grass enclosed in cloth tied to the middle of a beaded necklace.","role_refs":["role:7"],"evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"fig:12","name_or_label":"owner of the evil charm","description":"The person who preserves the treated liver in a buckskin bag on his body and uses incantations against a victim.","role_refs":["role:7"],"evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"fig:13","name_or_label":"victim of the evil charm","description":"The person at whom the evil charm is directed.","role_refs":["role:9"],"evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"fig:14","name_or_label":"Gwi'damba^bi","description":"A man who wears a weasel foot on his hat as woman-medicine to help him catch a woman.","role_refs":["role:8"],"evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"fig:15","name_or_label":"baby","description":"A baby whose neck is protected by a buckskin bag filled with powdered spruce needles.","role_refs":["role:7"],"evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"fig:16","name_or_label":"adults","description":"Adults who use white weaselskins, a white weasel foot, buffalo horns, and manes as safeguards against illness.","role_refs":["role:7"],"evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"fig:17","name_or_label":"Ross Fork Shoshone visitor","description":"A visitor who paid for the love-charm roots and was later seen married.","role_refs":["role:8"],"evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"fig:18","name_or_label":"desired woman","description":"The woman at whom the root-and-stone charm is thrown and who later comes to the man, looks into his eyes, and laughs.","role_refs":["role:10"],"evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"fig:19","name_or_label":"woman later married by the Ross Fork married.","role_refs":["role:10"],"evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"fig:20","name_or_label":"Lame-Jack","description":"A man who confirms Jack's statements and reports a deadly root of the same name.","role_refs":["role:6"],"evidence_refs":["ev:11"]}],"roles":[{"id":"role:1","label":"medicine-man","assigned_to":["fig:1","fig:4"],"basis":"Ko'bitsak and Tu'-dzomo-n-d5'mi are identified in treatment.","evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2"]},{"id":"role:3","label":"patient","assigned_to":["fig:2","fig:4"],"basis":"The child dies and Tu'-dzomo-n-d5'mi is taken sick and dies.","evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2"]},{"id":"role:4","label":"agent of mind or soul theft","assigned_to":["fig:5","fig:6"],"basis":"The dzo'ap snatches away the mind; Coyote carries off a man's across.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Nu'numbi is said to appear and disappear at will, and meeting him is taken as a sign of and that the theft-of-fire tale links Shoshone mythology with tribes west of the Rocky Mountains.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The comparative discussion lists The main tale concerns a poor boy raised by his grandmother who finds a speaking colt by a pond, defeats a chief in repeated races and a fire ordeal, captures a gigantic horse when his colt enlarges, and crosses a great sea to bring back a young woman.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A giant bird swoops down on a White man, carries him home, and cannot kill him.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The black monster's son comes home and wants to eat the sheep-raiser.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The White man uses a stick to knock down and kill both the monster and its son, then cuts off the monster's tail feathers and brings them home.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"An old woman lives with her grandson.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The boy plays by a pond, finds a colt and some gold there, and tends the colt every morning.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The colt speaks, asks for a halter, and tells the boy to race horses on the other side of the mountains.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"A Chief on the other side of the mountains has five daughters and five horses and agrees to race the boy.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The little horse wins repeated races over courses marked by mountains and colored goal markers, and Coyote seizes the Chief's horses after each victory.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The Chief proposes a contest of riding through a fire; the boy passes through unburned, while the Chief's horse falls and burns to death.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"For another task, the boy's colt grows larger than a gigantic horse, throws it down, and allows the boy to halter and lead it home before becoming small again.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"For a last task, the Chief tells the boy to bring back a young girl from beyond a big sea and promises him chiefship and property if he succeeds.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The boy crosses the sea on the disappears.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Several days later, at sunset near pine-trees, the narrator hears crying like that of a woman at a funeral while the narrator identifies it as a ghost and flees on horseback to his two friends.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"As a boy, the narrator flashes sunlight from a cease.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"After crossing a creek, the narrator is chased by a rattlesnake that ignores thrown stones; he thinks it may be a ghost {"record_id":"batch.motif.native-american-pawnee-mythology-dorsey-archive-l587-l627","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/native-american-plains/project-gutenberg/pawnee-mythology-dorsey.md","passage_locator":{"label":"MYTHS. / CONTENTS  3 / PREFACE. / INTRODUCTION.; lines 587-627","start":"587","end":"627","translation":"The Pawnee - Mythology (Part I)","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage gives an editorial summary of Pawnee tradition and ethnographic history: Chaui, Pitahauirat, and Kitkehahki are said to have once formed a single band called Kawarahkis, later separated geographically, retained closely related origin myths, borrowed some rites from the Skidi, and in recent decades became more unified again through removal to Oklahoma and shared ceremonial life.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The passage states that the Chaui, Pitahauirat, and Kitkehahki were originally a single band or division called the Kawarahkis.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"This earlier union is placed before the arrival of whites and is presented as a historic tradition.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The Kawarahkis are said to have lived near the present site of Nemaha in southeastern Nebraska near the Missouri River.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"After separation, the Kitkehahki went north to the Republican River, the Chaui went northwest and settled south of the Platte River, and the remnant near Nemaha later became known as the Pitahauirat and also migrated northwest.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The passage says the Chaui, Pitahauirat, and Kitkehahki are remnants of what was once a single tribe, and it cites the Arikara and Skidi as another case believed to have once formed a single tribe.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The origin myths of the three bands are described as practically the same, with some variation attributed to ceremonies or rites and accompanying origin stories acquired generally from the Skidi.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The tales of the four bands are said to form a unit today because of close association over the last forty years, removal to Oklahoma, treatment as a single tribe by the government, and mutual visits during ceremonies where storytelling is a regular feature.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Chaui","description":"One of the bands said to have originally belonged to the Kawarahkis; after separation it went northwest and settled south of the Platte River.","role_refs":["role:1"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Pitahauirat","description":"A band described as the remnant that remained near Nemaha for a long period and later became known as the Pitahauirat before migrating northwest.","role_refs":["role:1"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Kitkehahki","description":"One of the bands said to have originally belonged to the Kawarahkis; after separation it located on the Republican River.","role_refs":["role:1"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"Kawarahkis","description":"The earlier single band or division from which the Chaui, Pitahauirat, and Kitkehahki are said to derive; it lived near Nemaha.","role_refs":["role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2"]},{"id":"fig:5","name_or_label":"Skidi","description":"A band or tradition from which the other bands are said generally to have acquired certain ceremonies or rites and accompanying origin stories; the passage also says the other bands differ considerably from the Skidi.","role_refs":["role:3","role:4"],"evidence_refs":["ev:3","ev:4","ev:5"]},{"id":"fig:6","name_or_label":"Arikara","description":"A people cited as part of a comparison that the Arikara and Skidi may once have formed a single tribe.","role_refs":["role:4"],"evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"fig:7","name_or_label":"The four Pawnee bands","description":"The four bands whose tales are said to form TRUE  STORIES  OF  THE  HEAVENLY  BEINGS.; lines 915-971","start":"915","end":"971","translation":"The Pawnee - Mythology (Part I)","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"A woman and man complete and consecrate a lodge by offering corn, fat, and a skull. Tirawa explains that the earth is to be called mother, that the lodge represents a mother's breast, and that smoke, cooked food, life, death, and burial are all tied to this maternal image. Tirawa then instructs the woman to boil speckled corn in water over fire; after the couple eat the mush, they have increase. Tirawa gives ceremonies, including the Woman-dance and the Starisu. The passage then describes preparations for the Starisu ceremony: buffalo are hunted for meat, a chief's lodge is cleared, priests and a chief assemble, young men and girls of high birth are invited, and the chief says Tirawa promised buffalo if the dance is performed. Buffalo grease is applied because the dancers are about to imitate buffalo.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"After the lodge is post.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The man kills an animal, takes its fat, greases the four posts, and places the skull on the altar.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Tirawa says the earth is to be called mother and that the lodge represents the mother's increase.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Tirawa gives many ceremonies; two are said to have been handed down through all generations, including the Woman-dance, which reminds the people that Tirawa gave them light.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"For the Starisu ceremony, buffalo are killed for meat, the meat is dried, a content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.native-american-pawnee-mythology-dorsey-archive-l3132-l3178","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/native-american-plains/project-gutenberg/pawnee-mythology-dorsey.md","passage_locator":{"label":"II.  HOW  THE  PEOPLE  GOT  THE  CROW-LANCE.' / THE  ORIGIN  OF  THE  PIPE-STICK  CEREMONY.  53 / THE  GIRL  WHO  MARRIED  A  STAR.  57 / THE   GRAIN-OF-CORN  BUNDLE.  59; lines 3132-3178","start":"3132","end":"3178","translation":"The Pawnee - Mythology (Part I)","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage concludes an account of a meteor event: the people fear the world is ending, remember Pahokatawa's words, later discover a heavy multicolored turtle-shaped stone identified as a promised meteor, honor it with tobacco and pipe smoke, keep it with the Morning-Star bundle, and believe it gives war success and protection from disease. The passage then begins the tale 'Buffalo-Wife and Corn-Wife' with a young man who avoids herding and war parties and climbs a hill daily to sit on a pile of stones.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The people became afraid and mourned because they thought the world was coming to an end.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"A leader told the people to remember the words of Pahokatawa, and after recalling them the people decided it was not yet time.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The people went out to try to catch the meteors, and some old people later said the stars flew around like birds.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"During a buffalo hunt, two men came to a barren, smooth, round place with no grass, where a colored stone projected from the center.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"When the men dug out the stone, it had the shape of a turtle with legs, head, and eyes imprinted on it.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Big-Eagle said that Pahokatawa had promised the people a meteor.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The people retrieved the meteor with ponies; it was very heavy, and only a few people were allowed to see it.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"When the object was brought into the village, people offered tobacco and smoke to it, and priests offered pipe smoke.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Old people believed the meteor was part of the Morning-Star, and it was kept with the Morning-Star     "quote": "",
    "summary": "In this excerpt of \"Buffalo-Wife and Corn-Wife,\" Without-Wings survives a sweat-lodge attack, passes a lightning test at an eagle tree, defeats an old Buffalo cow in a race tied to the human-buffalo relation, drives buffalo out from a cave while rejecting some kinds, drinks the chief's wife's water, kills the bony Buffalo chief with help from a mocking-bird, and returns to his own people.",

      "id": "obs:1",
      "text": "In the sweat-lodge, the old woman uses a large buffalo-horn spoon to pour water on hot stones so that steam comes down on the naked bodies.",

      "evidence_refs": ["ev:1"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:2",
      "text": "The man turns himself into a Badger and digs into the ground until only his mouth and head remain above ground.",
      "category": "action",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:1"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:3",
      "text": "Without-Wings tells the old woman to pour on more water; she stops the attempt, and buffalo bulls around the sweat-lodge run away when he comes out uninjured.",
      "category": "sequence",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:1"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:4",
      "text": "The old woman sends Without-Wings for wood to a place with a tree bearing an Eagle's nest, and a storm with lightning gathers over him there.",
      "category": "sequence",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:2"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:5",
      "text": "After Without-Wings speaks to the Eagles and tells them who he is, the lightning stops and the storm passes.",
      "category": "action",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:2"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:6",
      "text": "The old Buffalo cow says a race to the four world quarters will decide whether people may live upon buffalo or buffalo upon people.",
      "category": "speech",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:3"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:7",
      "text": "Without-Wings turns himself into a Magpie, while the old woman uses a cane to move as far as her eye can see in a single step; Badgers dig holes so that she falls repeatedly.",
      "category": "sequence",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:3"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:8",

      "category": "action",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:4"]
    },

      "id": "obs:9",

      "category": "action",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:5"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:10",

      "category": "sequence",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:6", "ev:7"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:11",

      "category": "attribute",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:7"]
    },

In spring Ready-to-Give returns with corn, squash, and bean seeds, instructs the household to plant, and teaches the boy to make a ritual bundle. He also prescribes tobacco offerings to a winter buffalo bull and the ritual treatment of its skull, saying that he himself, as the Wind, will dwell in the skull. After teaching the bundle ceremonies for many months, he departs again, and a starving hunter from the people's group approaches the camp.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Ready-to-Give says that his boy will rule the people and can call the buffalo by invoking They search for their father, and a Mouse plus a speaking wood mortar reveal a hidden route; the boys descend through the opening into an underground world and continue following their father's trail through villages.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The father fears that the boys will try to kill him, tries to run away, realizes the strange boy's power is watching him, and returns to the lodge.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"After hunting for several days and bringing back deer and buffalo, ground.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"At an elm tree, the two boys disappear and find themselves in a lodge under the ground that is really a wood rat's nest, earth.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A man identified with Hawk enters a tipi in the valley and finds a man, a woman, four girls, and woman and that her ears hang down.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Young-Duck says an old woman bewitched her, says she will always live that way, and tells her husband and parents not to weep for her.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Young-Duck instructs Hawk to carry her high into the sky, drop her, and then fly to where beans.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The next day Hawk turns into a hawk again, carries Young-Duck on his back into the heavens, drops her, and then finds her He follows his brother's path, enters the settlement, refuses meals of human eyes and human ears disguised as squash, and delays the gambling match. On the fourth night he goes to a field of buffalo bones, cries over the skulls, sings for gaming sticks and a ring, and receives help from buffalo beings, one of whom leaves behind a stick that says it will defeat the gambler.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Raven returns and tells the younger brother that his brother is dead and that his head is at the gambler's lodge.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The boy starts out to seek his brother, uses his powers to see well, follows his brother's tracks, and sleeps where his brother slept.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"At the settlement, people warn the boy that the gambler will offer him human eyes to eat and advise him to carry the bowl away instead of eating.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The boy goes to the gambler's lodge, refuses the bowl of eyes, agrees to play the stick game, and postpones the game until the fifth day.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"On the third day the boy is warned that dried human ears will be presented as squash; he takes the bowl away and his hosts throw the contents out.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"On the fourth day the boy asks where buffalo wallows and bones can be found, and he is shown a hillside where many buffalo bones lie.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"At night the boy goes among buffalo skeletons, cries, and sings to an old bull skull asking for sticks and a ring.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The old bull says that the buffalo want to help get I99 / THE    SINGING    HAWK.  20I / THE  BOY  WHO  MARRIED  A  BUFFALO.; lines 10179-10198","start":"10179","end":"10198","translation":"The Pawnee - Mythology (Part I)","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"A young woman and a young man meet while traveling and discover that each has been seeking the other: he seeks a girl who dislikes men, and she seeks a man who dislikes women. She says she likes him, later tells her people about him, and an old Buffalo tells her to bring him. She returns at dawn, stands on a knoll, and sings. An attached note says the tale is efficacious for drawing buffalo near a village and mentions a blackbird that married a buffalo cow.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A young girl asks a young man where he is going.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The young man says he is going west to the other villages.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The girl says she is going to the lower village to visit the young man who dislikes women.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The young man says he is going to another village to see the young girl who dislikes men, and the girl says she is that girl.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The young man gives his name as Streaks-of-Black-Paint-across-Face-and-Legs.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The girl says she dislikes men but likes him, and the two then separate and go home.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The girl tells her people about the fine young man she saw.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"An old Buffalo tells the girl to go to the other village and bring the young man.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"At dawn the girl goes back to the lower village, stands on a little knoll on the north side, and sings.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"An editorial note says the tale teaches that such deeds may draw buffalo near the village and explains that a blackbird may perch on buffalo backs because it married a buffalo cow.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"young girl","description":"A young girl who says she village.","figure_refs":["fig:1","fig:3","fig:4"],"symbol_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"scene:3","label":"return and song at dawn","summary":"The girl returns at dawn, stands on a small   BUFFALO   AND   RED-SPIDER-WOMAN  S    DAUGHTER.  213 / TALES  OF  READY-TO-GIVE. / THE  BUFFALO  AND  THE  DEER.  215 / THE    HUNGRY   COYOTE.; lines 10852-10961","start":"10852","end":"10961","translation":"The Pawnee - Mythology (Part I)","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"This passage contains the end of a Coyote tale in which a calf flatters a hungry Coyote and escapes, after which Coyote dies on a sunny hillside; a full tale about priests opening a sacred bundle, women bringing wood and willows, and the youngest girl preparing mush for the priests before buffalo meat is later brought; and the beginning of another tale describing winter as the season for Coyote stories, singing, and children dancing in the lodges.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A calf addresses Coyote by singing that his name is He-who-Lets-them-Pass-Unharmed.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The calf says its own name is Poor-Pitiful-Calf and also calls Coyote Takes-Pity-upon-the-Weak.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"While Coyote is talking, the calf thinks about what to do, goes by, and begins to run fast.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Coyote then thinks he is hungry and that he should have killed and eaten the calf, and he calls after it.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The calf is already far away; Coyote cries, goes to a hillside where the sun shines, lies down, sleeps, and dies.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The narrator states that this is why coyotes are found lying on hillsides and dying of hunger.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"In a Coyote village, people decide to open their sacred bundle, and the young men ride out on ponies to kill buffalo.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"A crier goes through the village telling the women to bring dry wood and green willow branches to the lodge of the priests.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The youngest girl left in camp pounds corn into fine meal, boils it into mush, and brings a kettle of mush to the lodge.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The errand man receives the mush, the priests thank the girl, and the high priest says they will sing before eating it.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5","ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"After the young men later kill buffalo, some meat is brought to the priests, and the bundle is folded and hung at the altar.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"In winter, people in many lodges laugh, sing, tell Coyote stories, and make children dance.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"A young man goes from lodge to lodge hearing Coyote stories and goes hunting the next day.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Coyote","description":"A hungry Coyote who accepts the calf's flattering names, lets it pass, then It then begins a tale about a wonderful young man who goes to the village of Spider-Woman, where an old woman warns him that Spider-Woman kills young men and serves human body parts disguised as food.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A man in the hills saw a Coyote coming out from a hollow, drew his bow, then lowered it because he remembered it was bad luck to shoot a Coyote.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The man called to Coyote, said people talked about Coyotes during winter, and asked Coyote to tell him a story because they were alone in the hills.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Coyote stopped and sat on the snow; the man threw a stick at him, and Coyote ran away without barking.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"As Coyote ran, the man sang several times about Coyote, tallow, and having a story of the Whistling home in the Kiowa country.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Coyote disappeared, and afterward the man was always lucky in killing game; he thought this was because he had not shot at Coyote.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"In a village there lived a boy known as wonderful who wore his buffalo robe in a peculiar way, with the hair inside and only part of it showing over his shoulders.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"People reported that young men went to another village and never returned; in that village Spider-Woman contested with strangers in climbing an old cottonwood tree.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"After hearing of Spider-Woman many times, the young man decided to visit her village and traveled through thick willows until he reached a grass-lodge at the village edge.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"A youngest child saw the stranger and told his mother, who invited the young man into the lodge; he placed his quiver in the west of the lodge and sat down.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The old woman warned the young man that Spider-Woman took the lives of young men and used Eyes-Wide-Open to look into lodges for strangers and invite them to her lodge.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The old woman said that Spider-Woman's mush, black corn, and chopped squash were really human brains, eyes, and ears.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Eyes-Wide-Open came to invite the young man to eat with Spider-Woman, and the old woman whispered that he was taking the boy to be killed.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"man who sang to Coyote","description":"A man alone in the hills who saw Coyote, spared it, it.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The young man mixes tobacco, other roots, and sumach leaves in his own pipe, and after smoking it the old man becomes very He returns with magically produced plums, a bow from Mountain-Lion, and four colored arrows with flint points, but Stone-Man rejects each gift and demands still more.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Stone-Man tells his children not to stir, move, or It then narrates the origin of the Buffalo Medicine Dance: a buffalo attacks the holy lodge, a storm follows, buffalo restore sacred objects, and medicine-men are led into the Buffalo lodge through water, where animal beings perform wonders and give a skull-centered ceremony. The passage then opens a third account about a pregnant woman left behind, who gives birth alone, travels west with her child, and meets a buffalo bull that offers a healing root.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Howling-Fox stayed behind after the buffalo hunt, and Buffalo-Woman visited him at night, taught him Buffalo dance songs, and gave him the Buffalo ceremony.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"In the dance Howling-Fox wore on his left arm a ring taken from a Buffalo cow, gave presents and a pony to the ring's former owner, taught him the ceremony and songs, and later died; people said his death came after he had given away all his secrets.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"During a buffalo hunt the people camped in a valley, and the holy lodge containing the sacred bundle stood in the center of the village.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"A buffalo bull ran into the holy tipi where the bundle was hanging and tore the tipi to pieces.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"After the attack, dark clouds came, rain and storm followed, the wind blew one woman away, and later a buffalo spoke to the people and said their ritual things would be returned.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"A Buffalo invited some Buffalo medicine-men to go with him, led them far from the village to a steep bank, and they followed him into the Buffalo lodge through deep water.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Inside the animals' lodge, a Bear and a Buffalo performed sleight-of-hand; other animals sat around; animals blew their breath and soft downy feathers fell from their mouths; one Buffalo swallowed a reed whistle and later threw up feathers.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"A Buffalo told the men to keep a buffalo skull, give presents to it, and rely on dreams from the Buffalo spirit in the skull to know what to do in the ceremony.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The men returned to the village, performed the ceremony, and first sang the song taught by the Buffalo.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"A young woman who was pregnant and abandoned in the village gave birth alone, remained with the child, and then went west carrying the crying baby on her back.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"On a high hill the woman met a Buffalo bull in a hollow; the bull spoke with It then tells of a lost warrior who meets a singing buffalo cow on a hill before dawn, learns a song and the Big-Warrior dance, receives power, and gains success in war travel and pony capture. The passage then begins a story of a lonely boy who returns after an absence, sees a woman among buffalo, asks to marry her, and is told to bring a scalp and blue beads for the Buffalo.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Dust is taken from the center where the ring stops, carried home, smelled by a man, and rubbed over his head, arms, and legs so that he will get well.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"As the tribe increases, other people prepare meat and hold the game, and young boys make their own sticks and rings and play it themselves.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"A particular man performs a sleight-of-hand with a black stick in the medicine-man's lodge and draws smoke from a lit pipe bowl through the stick even though no hole can be found.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"A warrior on the war-path hides from pursuing enemies, comes out after they pass, believes he is lost, and cries out to the gods in the heavens and to the animal gods.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Before daylight, while climbing a high hill, the lost man hears singing from the east and sees a buffalo cow running toward him and snorting.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The buffalo tells the man not to be afraid, says she had been singing as she loped over the hills, and says she will teach him the song and that he will start a dance called the Big-Warrior dance.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The buffalo and the man sit together on the hilltop looking east, and as the sun rises the buffalo gallops toward the east singing the same song.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4","ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The man learns many mysterious things from the buffalo and receives power to travel without growing tired and to capture many ponies; he is told to sing the song at dawn.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"A boy cries because no woman loves him and he says he has not even a sister; after calling to the gods he disappears for one winter.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"In the spring the boy sees a large herd of buffalo with a woman among them, asks the woman to marry him, and she agrees.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The woman's uncle says he wants a scalp and blue beads to give to the Buffalo, and the boy goes to the chief's tipi to request them.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"unnamed sick man","description":"A man who is treated with dust taken from the center where the ring stops.","role_refs":["role:1"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"unnamed lodge performer","description":"A man who uses a black stick and a lit pipe in a In the story, a wounded man is left behind with food, water, and fire sticks. He repeatedly hears many voices and laughter while his meat is stolen. After his food is gone, Scalped-Man appears, offers healing, and carries him to a large cave. The cave contains sage, a fireplace, a decorated buffalo skull, stored meat, and robes. Scalped-Man repeatedly demonstrates that he can produce many voices and war cries, including voices the man mistakes for his parents and other people, and finally offers to give the man that sound-making power.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The framing note states that scalped people are believed to be able to confer power and that the story shows ventriloquism.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The wounded man is left behind when the camp moves, and his companions leave him dried buffalo meat, water, and fire sticks.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"After the war party leaves, the wounded man hears many voices and laughter, but he cannot see anyone.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Over several nights, portions of the wounded man's meat are stolen until none remains.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"After the last piece of meat is taken, Scalped-Man appears and says that he will heal the man's wounds and care for him cave.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Inside the cave are heaps of wild sage, a fireplace, a buffalo skull decorated with blue beads, eagle feathers, black silk handkerchiefs, and wampum, stores of dried meat, and buffalo robes.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The wounded man cannot see any opening in the cave and cannot tell how they entered it.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Each day Scalped-Man leaves the cave; before he returns, the wounded man hears many voices and war cries, and Scalped-Man says he made all the noise.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The wounded man thinks he hears his father, mother, and other people calling his name, gets up, and tries to find the entrance.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Scalped-Man later says that he made the voices, demonstrates many different The boy falls through an opening into an Eagles' den. The Eagles condemn the uncle's act, note the grief of the child's parents, consult their aged father and mother, refuse the man any power, and decide that the child will remain with them and be turned into an Eagle.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A man repeatedly goes to a high hill where many eagle feathers are scattered, stands by a soft downy feather at the top, cries there, and then gathers the feathers without receiving any power.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The first feathers the man finds are placed all over his robe.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"While the people are living on the Republican River, the man decides to learn what is in the hill and takes his little nephew away from the village.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The boy's parents search for him through the village and cannot find him.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"At the hill, the man places the boy on the downy place and says he gives his nephew to the being in that place to devour in return for pity, power, and instruction about the feathers.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The soft downy feather marks an opening through which eagles fly in and out, and the boy drops into that hole.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Inside the den, the Eagles whistle, jump up, and say the man has stolen his own nephew and placed him there for them to feast upon.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The Eagles say they had been arranging a time to admit the man to their den, but because he stole the child they will consult their old father and mother instead.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4","ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"On the east side of the den sit two very old Eagles, called the father and mother of the Eagles, with worn-off feathers.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The old man Eagle says the man sought the Eagles' power and secrets in haste, so they will not give him powers, and the boy will be turned into an Eagle.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"After the decision, the village.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Hot coals are placed on the east, south, west, and north sides of the boy, wild sage is put on stays with a poor old couple, hears of a powerful being who seizes the fattest buffalo, and ends with a sung summons for named men to go look for buffalo.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A repeated opening song says the daughters of Claw-Shield, Brave-Fox, and Jack-Rabbit come After failing several times to stand firm, he remains in a buffalo wallow, is struck by the Buffalo's charge, and becomes a Buffalo. The Buffalo teaches him buffalo ways, but when the transformed Coyote tries to make another Coyote into a Buffalo, he loses the power and becomes a Coyote again. He returns to the Buffalo, is transformed again, and is warned not to try to give that power to other Coyotes.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A starving Coyote meets a Buffalo bull grazing and asks for help because the Buffalo has grass to eat everywhere while Coyote has nothing to eat.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The Buffalo bull says he knows Coyote is tricky and warns that if he helps him, Coyote may do something wrong and be killed.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"At a buffalo wallow, the Buffalo bull charges Coyote several times; after Coyote finally stands firm, the Buffalo's strike turns him into a Buffalo.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"After the transformation, the Buffalo tells Coyote-Buffalo to stay with him, learn buffalo powers, graze on high hills, run when people approach, travel ravines at night, sit in weeds, and keep his nose toward the wind when resting.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"An editorial note says the story is told to children so they learn that power received from animals must be kept to oneself and not given to someone else, or the power will leave them.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Coyote-Buffalo tells another starving Coyote that he can make him into a Buffalo, but during the attempt he himself turns back into a Coyote and the two Coyotes lock mouths together.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Coyote returns to the Buffalo, is turned into a Buffalo again, and is told not to try turning Coyotes into Buffalo.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Coyote / Coyote-Buffalo","description":"A starving Coyote who is turned into a Buffalo, later Turtle hides the meat in an eagle nest high in a cottonwood tree, where Coyote dies trying to reach him after mistaking the reflection of Turtle's fire in water for Turtle below the surface. coyotes willing to help are not killed.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"Morning-Star gives the boy flint stone, and with it he removes the teeth from the girl's vagina; attackers.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Hawk, described as a great warrior, lives with his wife and feather transformation, and later becomes Buffalo; a blackbird youth marries a buffalo girl, after which buffalo are ritually sent to humans and made holy; and a poor boy is summoned by the buffalo chief's son to a buffalo dwelling beyond mountains in a cave.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"In the first abstract, the daughter of Buffalo chief visits a boy and his sister, and the boy has one red arrow and one black arrow.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The boy shoots a cow with an arrow that penetrates only beneath the skin and follows it in hopes of recovering the arrow.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"At night a tipi appears for the boy to sleep in; by morning it has become Buffalo, and on later nights he finds a woman there who tells him she loves him, feeds him, and spends the night with him as wife, while by morning she is Buffalo.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The boy and the Buffalo woman encounter an old bull, to which the boy offers tobacco, and then enter Buffalo village, where some receive him kindly and others are hostile.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The girl's uncle, White-Spot Buffalo, jumps at the boy and is shot, and the boy also kills the girl's father, who has a white spot on his forehead.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"When the buffalo try to kill the boy, each time he turns into breath feather.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The buffalo ask for sacrifice of smoke; certain buffalo are taken to the boy's village to be killed, their meat is made holy, their spirits return to Buffalo village, and the boy later becomes Buffalo.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"In the second abstract, a young boy who dislikes women escapes them as blackbird, while in the western Buffalo village there is a girl who dislikes men; each decides to visit the other and they meet on a high hill between villages.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The girl sings by a river bank about her lover, Coyote hears her and schemes to get her, but the boy arrives first, takes her to his tipi, and then to her father, who is glad and gives smoke.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The Buffalo chief sends eight buffalo, then larger numbers, to people to be killed; their meat is made holy, and eventually the buffalo scatter for the benefit of people.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Because Buffalo wife wore an elk dress, women in ceremonies wear such dress and also wear an eagle feather on their heads when a husband makes Buffalo holy.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Buffalo wife makes her husband angry, and he flies away as blackbird and then lives among Seeking death, the boy travels to a mysterious tipi where little people and animal beings, including Hawk, deliberate about helping him and carry him onward to another animal lodge.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A young boy plays by himself, imitates the ways of a doctor, and often succeeds.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"A powerful medicine-man of a neighboring tribe hears of the boy, is jealous, and visits him.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The medicine-man offers tobacco from a skunk-skin pouch, and he and the boy smoke together.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"On later visits, the old man and his wife bring presents and ask the boy to tell stories of his medicine.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The boy says he has no power, has never been initiated into a mysterious lodge, and does not know the source of his curative success.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"On the fourth night the old man again offers smoke; the boy faints, is awakened, and afterward feels something peculiar in his stomach and shows increasing signs of pregnancy.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4","ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The boy leaves to die in a strange country, traveling south and then west and going to dangerous places where he tempts wild animals to kill him.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5","ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"On a hill the boy hears noises, finds a large new tipi, is repeatedly warned not to approach, but enters and says he is willing to die.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Little people sit around the lodge, and on the south side there is a queerly dressed man with white streaks of paint on his face and lariats and downy feathers hanging over him.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Raccoon, muskrat, and two errand men are willing to help, other animal lodges must be consulted, and the south-side being content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.native-american-pawnee-mythology-dorsey-archive-l25545-l25596","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/native-american-plains/project-gutenberg/pawnee-mythology-dorsey.md","passage_locator":{"label":"ABSTRACTS.  509 / ABSTRACTS.  51I / ABSTRACTS.  513 / ABSTRACTS.  JIS; lines 25545-25596","start":"25545","end":"25596","translation":"The Pawnee - Mythology (Part I)","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The excerpt closes a Stone-Man episode in which Stone-Man is broken apart after a failed buffalo hunt, his fragments are thrown into a boiling spring, and a Stone-Medicine lodge is later founded around a saved stone remnant. It then summarizes two medicine traditions: one revealed through a giant's bone found near Swimming Mound, and another tied to a primeval giant race destroyed by flood, whose remains and root-derived medicine retain power.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Stone-Man shoots at a buffalo repeatedly, but the arrow points stop in the buffalo's hair, and he empties multiple quivers.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The last four arrows are described as colored and made only of rushes.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"After Stone-Man runs past it, the buffalo rises and hooks him, and pieces of stone fall from him whistling through the air.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The young man's two errand men batter Stone-Man to pieces while the girl throws the pieces into a boiling spring.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Steam from the spring fills the lodge and rises from the top; by morning the lodge has become a solid stone earth-lodge, and the account links this to geysers in the west.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The young man takes his wife home, starts an animal-lodge, and the lodge is known as the Stone-Medicine lodge because a stone piece saved by the girl is kept on the altar.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The saved altar stone is said to be part of the girl's father, and after it is lost in a river during a Sioux attack, the ceremony is transmitted to the couple's children.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"A hunter sleeping on a hill near Swimming Mound is addressed by a giant, who says many giant people drowned there and directs him to a thigh bone on the south side of the hill.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The found bone is carved with a man and woman, a skull, a bow and arrows, many stars, and also the sun and moon.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The giant later teaches the man in a dream how to hold a ceremony and what songs to sing; the man becomes a medicine-man and uses dust from the bone in doctoring.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"During a smallpox epidemic, those who touch the bone are said to be immune.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"A former race of giants is said to have reviled the sun and thunder, after which Tirawa sends rain and waters that cover the earth and wash the giants away.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"The washed-away giants sink into soft earth on steep banks and high places, and their bones are said to retain healing power for later medicines.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:7","ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Big-Black-Meteoric-Star tells a man to dig a great root that sprang from a giant and explains how to obtain and prepare it.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"The root is feared because of its human-like odor, but the man digs it while singing taught songs and other people join him.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Stone-Man","description":"A stone-bodied being who hunts buffalo, is hooked by the buffalo, broken into pieces, and later survives as a saved stone remnant on an altar.","role_refs":["role:1"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2","ev:3"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Buffalo","description":"The buffalo at which Stone-Man shoots and which rises, hooks him, and knocks pieces from him.","role_refs":["role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Young man","description":"The man whose two errand men help destroy Stone-Man; he later takes his wife home, starts a lodge, and performs miracles.","role_refs":["role:3"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:3"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"Girl / wife","description":"The girl who throws Stone-Man's pieces into the boiling spring, later the young man's wife, who saves a stone piece identified as part of her father.","role_refs":["role:4"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:3"]},{"id":"fig:5","name_or_label":"Two errand men","description":"Two attendants of the young man who batter Stone-Man to collected rings as buffalo approach.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A man frightens enemies by waving his shield, robe, and spear, orders his side to attack, becomes famous, marries the chief's daughter, and becomes chief of the tribe.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"A jealous young man bears false witness about the husband to the girl's brother.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The husband tells his brother-in-law not to ride a black or dun horse while hunting, but the young man rides a dun horse on a buffalo hunt and both rider and horse are killed.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The husband learns by magic power what happened, has the boy placed on the east side of the village, and at sunrise black and dun horses run over the boy; the wife then wakes her brother and restores him to their father.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"To prove his power on the war-path, the man throws his lariat over his shoulder, a storm comes from the heavens, covers the enemy, and his party captures the enemy's horses.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"When the village is attacked, the man throws his spear among the enemy, it makes a great noise, and a deep ravine opens between the enemy and the village.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The man says that when black and dun horses fight together in the same battle he must die; he and his brother-in-law are then both killed with their horses, and his wife gives his lariat and other belongings to one of their sons, who becomes a medicine-man and continues the wild horse dance.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Howling Fox hears a rumbling noise pass east beneath the playgrounds and then west again in the evening, and in the night he is told to remain on the playground the next day.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"After bathing and going to the grounds with pipe and tobacco, Howling Fox is addressed by a woman coming from the west, and he recognizes her as buffalo.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The buffalo woman says she has six sons and one daughter, that the daughter is missing, and that the missing daughter is the ring used by one of the gamblers; she promises Howling Fox great power if he finds her.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Howling Fox borrows gaming rings, places them west of the fireplace in his lodge, makes smoke offerings to the heavens and to the rings, hides them under his pillow, then places them on the north side of the grounds and hears rumbling and hoof sounds approaching from beneath the ground.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"chief's son-in-law / husband","description":"A powerful man who becomes famous in battle, marries the chief's daughter, restores his brother-in-law, commands storm and ravine effects, and later dies on a black horse.","role_refs":["role:1"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2","ev:3","ev:4","ev:5"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"chief's daughter / wife","description":"The woman married to the powerful man; she wakes her brother after the horse-trampling episode and later keeps her husband's belongings for their children.","role_refs":["role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2","ev:5"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"chief / father-in-law","description":"The chief whose daughter marries the powerful man and to whom the restored son is returned.","role_refs":["role:3"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"chief's son / brother-in-law","description":"The wife's brother, warned not {"record_id":"batch.motif.native-american-pawnee-mythology-dorsey-archive-l26291-l26334","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/native-american-plains/project-gutenberg/pawnee-mythology-dorsey.md","passage_locator":{"label":"ABSTRACTS.  523 / ABSTRACTS.  525 / ABSTRACTS.  527 / ABSTRACTS.  529; lines 26291-26334","start":"26291","end":"26334","translation":"The Pawnee - Mythology (Part I)","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage gives an abstract account of a game-and-medicine complex revealed in sleep and tied to buffalo, stars, sun, moon, Tirawa, the earth, and the cardinal directions, followed by a brief account of a lost warrior who gains buffalo medicine and war success from a singing buffalo cow.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A man whose medicines are herbs sleeps outdoors, sees stars that appear as sticks and rings of the javelin game, and in sleep is told by a man to make the game and play it on the west side of the village; east is linked with diseases, south with the dead, and north with enemies.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"He is instructed to make an ash bow and dogwood arrows, kill two buffalo bulls for hides to wrap two javelins, and cut the tree on north, east, south, and finally west before felling it.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The long sticks are to be the length of his body and represent men, while two shorter sticks represent one-horned buffalo in the west, and the sticks are spliced in pairs.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"He kills a buffalo cow, places her head toward the east, and uses skin from around the vulva to make a ring.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The gaming sticks are shaped to represent ears and a single horn, with two cross sticks tied on as legs; the front cross stick represents the sun and the hind one the moon, and the moon is said to have won the first game in the heavens and given the sticks to men.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"One prepared stick is charred black to represent darkness, night, or north, and the other is left white to represent light, day, or south; a white bead on the ring represents the star that gave the game, and the ring is carried by the man's granddaughter.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"At the gaming ground they smoke to the star, the earth, the ring, and the javelin; they count to one hundred and twenty; the losing side furnishes fire to boil meat for an offering; pieces of heart and tongue are offered to the sun, moon, and stars; and the game and player are rubbed with fat.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Later he is told to make another ring from a buffalo calf and add a blue bead representing Tirawa, with the ring representing earth; dust from the center of the ring is used in doctoring, other men imitate the set, and the black javelin is used in the medicine-lodge as a pipe-stem.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"In the later abstract, warriors are taken by an enemy, one hides, loses his way while returning home, and cries to spirits.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"On a hill he hears a buffalo cow singing in the east; she teaches him many mysteries and gives him power to travel without fatigue and capture ponies, and after learning her song he is always successful on the war-path.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Herb-medicine man and owner of the gaming set","description":"A man whose medicines are herbs receives instructions in sleep, makes the gaming equipment, oversees play and offerings, and later uses the black javelin in the medicine-lodge.","role_refs":["role:1"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2","ev:5","ev:6"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Dream visitor","description":"A man appears in sleep and tells the herb-medicine man how to make and where to play the game.","role_refs":["role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Star or stars","description":"Stars appear as sticks and rings, a star is  539 / ABSTRACTS.  54I / ABSTRACTS.  543 / ABSTRACTS.  545; lines 27088-27169","start":"27088","end":"27169","translation":"The Pawnee - Mythology (Part I)","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"A sequence of brief animal-tale abstracts: Coyote is undone after eating Artichoke; Chief Coyote's severed organ becomes plum trees, grape vines, berry bushes, and nut trees; Skunks deceive and kill Beaver medicine-men until a surviving Beaver is taken underwater to the others; Wild-Cat kills Bear and recovers her young, while Coyote falsely claims the kill; Rabbit loses and regains his tail with Turtle's help; Magpie directs two rats to food sources; Turtle escapes captors by pretending to fear water; and Rabbit, Turtle, and Spider-Woman are killed by foxes using firebrands and clubs.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Coyote is challenged by Artichoke to bite it, does so, and devours it.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Coyote begins to expel increasing flatus, is lifted from the ground, and is washed away by his own excrement.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Coyotes are said to have once had membrums long enough to go around the waist and to send them into water so that women would think they were snakes and flee.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Chief Coyote unwinds his membrum, puts it into a hole in the ground, and it is gnawed into pieces.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Chief Coyote throws the recovered pieces in different directions, producing plum trees, grape vines, berry bushes, and nut trees, and an insect says coyotes will no longer have long membrums.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Skunks feign illness, summon Beaver medicine-men through an old woman, and kill them one after another for food.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The last Beaver is taken underwater by a diving bird to a lodge where the killed Beavers are found, after which Beavers live in water and people throw beaver bones into water so they may become beavers again.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Wild-Cat follows Bear, claws Bear's stomach open, removes her young ones, and later gives the bear carcass to Coyote, who falsely claims the kill and then dies of fright when an old bear passes by.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Rabbit loses his tail at a willow limb, recovers it where Turtle directs him to search, and Turtle restores it; willow thereafter bears white fur.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Magpie tells Black Rat where to find artichokes and White Rat where to find ground nuts, and rats use these for food thereafter.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Turtle on the war-path is captured, warns captors against throwing him into fire, pretends to fear water, and escapes when they throw him into water.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Rabbit, Turtle, and Spider-Woman go on the war-path against enemies whose camp is surrounded by skulls, boast of their power, and are killed by foxes carrying firebrands and war clubs.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Coyote (artichoke episode)","description":"A coyote on the road who bites and devours Artichoke and is carried off by gas and
